headline: European Flight Hoaxes Disrupted Flights Without Delaying the Network
deck: Diversions, escorts and searches affected individual flights, while Eurocontrol reported no network-wide delay impact and no author was identified.
body: Bomb threats targeted at least 21 aircraft and several European airports in the second such incident that week; the United Kingdom called it a malicious hoax. [E1]
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French air base, while Italian fighter jets escorted a Finnair Helsinki-to-Rome flight. [E2]
On Thursday, some 25 flights to cities in more than a dozen countries were disrupted by bomb threats. [E5]
Eurocontrol said threats were known on 14 flights on Thursday and seven on Tuesday. [E7]
Eurocontrol said the threats had so far had no impact on delays in Europe’s air-traffic network. [E6]
Searches found no explosives, and it remained unclear whether incidents claimed by a little-known group were related. [E3]
Warnings were signed for a group or individual calling themselves Fighters of the Male State and claimed an anti-feminist-regime motive. [E4]
AOL reported the assessment that the threats could be an attempt at hybrid aggression and psychological warfare. [E8]

**The desk's reading.** The diversions, escort and searches establish operational disruption at affected flights, but Eurocontrol’s network assessment means those incidents do not establish system-wide delay. The signed warnings are the strongest competing indication of a common author, yet a claimed name and motive do not identify an author or connect the second wave. The reported assessment offers a competing political reading, not an investigative attribution.

**The next test.** A public investigative finding that links the warnings to the same sender or shared technical evidence would support a common-author reading. A finding that identifies separate senders or independent origins would overturn it.
